title: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
description: Tests machine learning mathematical foundations, neural network architectures, transformers, backpropagation, and optimization.

questions.question: In the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, what is the primary structural effect of increasing model complexity (e.g. adding high-degree polynomial features or deeper layers)?
options: Bias increases while Variance decreases, causing systematic underfitting.
Bias decreases while Variance increases, making the model prone to overfitting on training noise.
Both Bias and Variance decrease simultaneously to zero.
Model complexity has no mathematical correlation with Variance.
questions.explanation: High model complexity fits training data tightly, lowering bias (training error) but elevating variance (generalization error on unseen validation sets) due to overfitting on noise.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between L1 Regularization (Lasso) and L2 Regularization (Ridge)?
options: L1 regularization penalizes the absolute sum of weights (|w|), driving irrelevant feature weights to exact zero and performing feature selection; L2 penalizes squared weights (w^2), shrinking weights smoothly toward zero without exact elimination.
L1 is only applicable to decision trees, while L2 is exclusive to neural networks.
L2 creates sparse weight vectors, whereas L1 preserves dense weights.
L1 eliminates the need for a learning rate in gradient descent.
questions.explanation: L1 (Lasso) penalty produces diamond-shaped constraint boundaries that intersect axes, producing sparse solutions with exact zeros (feature selection). L2 (Ridge) spherical constraints shrink weights evenly without driving them completely to zero.

questions.question: Why did Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) largely replace the Sigmoid activation function in deep neural network hidden layers?
options: Sigmoid produces negative values that crash matrix multiplication routines.

Sigmoid saturates at extreme values where its derivative approaches zero, causing the Vanishing Gradient problem during backpropagation in deep layers; ReLU maintains a constant gradient of 1 for positive inputs.
ReLU is a non-linear function that can only be evaluated on dedicated GPUs.
Sigmoid requires 100 times more parameters than ReLU.
questions.explanation: For inputs far from 0, the Sigmoid derivative sigma'(x) = sigma(x)(1 - sigma(x)) approaches 0. Multiplying small gradients across many layers via the chain rule causes gradients to vanish, stalling weight updates.

questions.question: When evaluating a disease detection or fraud classification model with extreme class imbalance (e.g. 99.9% negative, 0.1% positive), why is Accuracy a misleading metric?
options: Accuracy cannot be calculated on binary labels.
A naive model predicting 'negative' for 100% of samples achieves 99.9% accuracy while failing to identify a single critical positive case; Precision, Recall, and PR-AUC are far more informative.
Accuracy is only valid if the dataset contains equal numbers of features.
Accuracy always underestimates true model capability.
questions.explanation: With severe class imbalance, predicting the majority class yields high trivial accuracy. Recall (True Positive Rate) and Precision (Positive Predictive Value), alongside F1-score and PR-AUC, evaluate how effectively positive cases are captured.

questions.question: In the standard Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al.), what is the mathematical formula for Scaled Dot-Product Attention?
options: softmax(Q * K * V) / sqrt(d_k)
softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V
sigmoid(Q * K^T) + V
relu(Q * V^T) * K
questions.explanation: Queries Q and Keys K are dot-multiplied to obtain similarity logits, scaled by sqrt(d_k) to prevent softmax gradients from vanishing with large dimensions, normalized via softmax, and multiplied by Values V.

questions.question: What is the primary role of Pooling layers (e.g. Max Pooling) in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)?
options: To increase the color depth of input imagery.
To downsample spatial feature map dimensions, reducing parameters/computation while providing spatial translation invariance.
To replace fully connected layers at the end of the network.
To generate synthetic image data during training.
questions.explanation: Max pooling downsamples spatial height and width by picking the dominant activation in each kernel window. This decreases computational parameters and provides robustness against small translations of features.

questions.question: What mathematical principle powers the Backpropagation algorithm in neural networks?
options: Euler's Totient Theorem
The Chain Rule of multivariable calculus for calculating partial derivatives of the loss function with respect to weights across layers.
The Central Limit Theorem of Gaussian distributions.
Monte Carlo random sampling.
questions.explanation: Backpropagation recursively applies the Chain Rule backwards from the output loss through the computational graph to determine the gradient dL/dW for every trainable parameter in the network.

questions.question: What distinguishes the Adam optimizer from standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD)?
options: Adam computes exact Hessian second-order derivatives.
Adam combines Momentum (exponential moving average of past gradients) with RMSProp (exponential moving average of squared gradients) for adaptive per-parameter learning rates.
Adam eliminates the need for backpropagation entirely.
Adam requires batch size to equal total dataset size.
questions.explanation: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) tracks both the first moment (mean of past gradients) and the second moment (uncentered variance of squared gradients) with bias corrections, adapting learning rates per parameter.

questions.question: What is the core distinction between Random Forest (Bagging) and Gradient Boosting (e.g. XGBoost)?
options: Random Forest builds deep independent trees in parallel and averages predictions to reduce Variance; Gradient Boosting trains shallow trees sequentially, each learning to predict the residual errors of prior trees to reduce Bias.
Random Forest is for regression only, while Gradient Boosting is only for classification.
Gradient Boosting trains trees in parallel without sequential dependencies.
Random Forest requires neural network activations.
questions.explanation: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregation in Random Forests) builds independent models in parallel from bootstrap samples, reducing variance. Boosting builds models sequentially where each weak learner corrects pseudo-residuals of predecessors, reducing bias.

questions.question: How does the 'Dropout' regularization technique function during neural network training?
options: It removes 50% of the training dataset before every epoch.
It randomly deactivates (zeros out) a fraction p of hidden neuron activations during forward passes, preventing co-adaptation of features.
It permanently prunes dead weights after each epoch.
It resets model weights to zero if the loss stops decreasing.
questions.explanation: During training, Dropout randomly turns off neurons with probability p. This forces other units to learn redundant, generalized representations rather than co-depending on specific neighbor activations. At test time, all neurons are active with scaled weights.
